sourcingNotes: Sibling pack run-1707/facts-1707.json (verified 2026-09-23) was read first; its case law (Eatmon v. Weeks for Georgia, Collins v. Frasier / Boyleston v. Baxley for South Carolina), its Georgia DDS / § 40-5-35 / Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 375-3-5 findings and its SCDMV § 56-1-221 findings are reused here with the same canonical URLs. Nothing in this post touches physician liability (Gilhuly / Hardee) or insurance (§ 33-7-11, §§ 38-77-150/160), so those citations are not carried into this pack; the post makes no insurance claim at all.

Epilepsy statistics: data/statistics.json has no epilepsy or seizure entry, so both figures were verified directly against CDC pages. The CDC facts-stats page (2021-2022 NHIS) gives about 2.9 million adults and about 456,000 children with active epilepsy; the 'less than half seizure-free' figure is from CDC's MMWR of April 20, 2018 (Tian et al.), analysing 2013 and 2015 NHIS data: among adults with active epilepsy taking medication, 42.4% were seizure-free in 2015 (45.3% in 2013; 44% pooled). Neither figure is in the registry; the refresh may cite them in-text with the vintage but should not add them to statistics.json without owner review.

Georgia seizure rule is primary-sourced twice over: O.C.G.A. § 40-5-35 (a noncommercial Class C license 'shall not be' denied for epilepsy 'unless such an episode occurred within the immediately preceding six-month period'; physicians 'may report' and are immune) and Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 375-3-5-.02 (Alterations of Consciousness; six months for epilepsy; Group A/B one-year framework; limited license for Group B only for 'Nocturnal epilepsy and stress hypoglycemia'). Rule text read on rules.sos.ga.gov and law.cornell.edu/regulations/georgia; the Georgia DDS Medical Review Process page supplies the reporting-sources sentence the post paraphrases.

South Carolina seizure rule: NO seizure-free period exists in statute or regulation. Title 56 Chapter 1 (scstatehouse.gov, downloaded in full) contains no occurrence of 'epilep', 'seizure' or 'lapse of consciousness'; the S.C. Code of Regulations chapter 63 index has no medical-fitness regulation. What South Carolina has is (1) S.C. Code § 56-1-40(4) (no license to a person 'who has a mental or physical condition which prevents him from safely operating a motor vehicle'), (2) § 56-1-130(A) (DMV 'may require a further physical and mental examination'), (3) § 56-1-270 (with 'good cause to believe' a licensee is unfit 'because of physical or mental disability', DMV may on ten days' written notice require an examination and suspend, revoke or restrict; refusal is itself grounds), (4) § 56-1-221 (Medical Advisory Board advises DMV on 'medical criteria'; the driver may submit a report from a physician of his choice), and (5) the license application itself, SCDMV Form 447-NC (Rev. 09/2025), question 5: 'In the past 12 months have you experienced a loss of consciousness, muscular control, or seizure?' and question 9 on any condition preventing safe operation. The 'six months' figure for South Carolina appears only in the Epilepsy Foundation's state chart (reproduced by the AAP, data as of November 2011: SC = 6 months, periodic updates 'annually for 3 years', doctors not required to report, appeal within 10 days). That is a secondary, 15-year-old source and the SCDMV publishes no such rule, so the refresh must NOT state a six-month period as South Carolina law; state the 12-month application question and the DMV's examination power instead.

Epilepsy Foundation pages (epilepsy.com) return Cloudflare 403 to every fetcher used; they are indexed by search engines and the AAP-hosted copy of the Foundation chart was read directly. law.justia.com and rules.sos.ga.gov return 403 to curl; the Georgia rule was read via WebFetch and Cornell LII, the Georgia statute on codes.findlaw.com. Justia URLs below are the site's canonical year-less form, not verified live in this run (same caveat as the sibling pack).

verifiedClaims.claim: The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reported in 2015 that less than half of those on medication were seizure-free.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: CDC's April 2018 MMWR analysis of 2015 survey data: 93.0% of U.S. adults with active epilepsy took epilepsy medication, and only 42.4% of those taking medication were seizure-free in the past year (45.3% in 2013; 'Among respondents taking epilepsy medication, 44% reported that their seizures were controlled in the past year' for the two years pooled).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Tian N, Boring M, Kobau R, Zack MM, Croft JB. Active Epilepsy and Seizure Control in Adults — United States, 2013 and 2015. MMWR 2018;67(15):437-442 (April 20, 2018)
verifiedClaims.note: 'Less than half' is correct; 'reported in 2015' is not. The data were collected in 2015 and the CDC published the finding in 2018. Rewrite as 'CDC data from 2015, published in 2018, found that ... fewer than half (about 42%) ... were seizure-free in the previous year' and link the word 'reported' (currently unlinked) to the MMWR URL. Denominator is adults taking medication, not all adults with epilepsy.

verifiedClaims.claim: In many states, individuals with epilepsy can obtain a driver's license if they haven't experienced a seizure within the last six months.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: GEORGIA: yes, by statute and rule. O.C.G.A. § 40-5-35: 'a person shall not be disqualified from obtaining a noncommercial Class C driver's license for having had an episode of lapsed or altered consciousness due to epilepsy unless such an episode occurred within the immediately preceding six-month period.' Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 375-3-5-.02: 'An individual who had an episode of altered consciousness due to epilepsy may be issued a Class C license, if otherwise qualified, if the episode did not occur within the last six months.' SOUTH CAROLINA: no seizure-free period is written into statute or regulation. The license application (SCDMV Form 447-NC, Rev. 09/2025) asks 'In the past 12 months have you experienced a loss of consciousness, muscular control, or seizure?' and whether you have 'any mental or physical condition preventing you from safely operating a motor vehicle'; the DMV may not license a person with such a condition (S.C. Code § 56-1-40(4)), may require a further physical and mental examination (§ 56-1-130), and decides medical fitness case by case with advice from its Medical Advisory Board (§ 56-1-221).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-5-35 (FindLaw text); Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 375-3-5-.02 (rules.sos.ga.gov; Cornell LII); SCDMV Form 447-NC (Rev. 09/2025); S.C. Code §§ 56-1-40, 56-1-130, 56-1-221 (scstatehouse.gov)
verifiedClaims.note: CONSEQUENTIAL for a two-state post. 'In many states ... six months' is true of Georgia and must be stamped as Georgia (noncommercial Class C only). It must NOT be stated for South Carolina: the only source giving SC a six-month period is the Epilepsy Foundation's state chart (data as of November 2011, reproduced by the AAP), which is secondary and 15 years old, and the SCDMV publishes no such rule. SC form URL: https://dmv.sc.gov/sites/scdmv/files/2026-01/447-NC_0.pdf.

verifiedClaims.claim: Those who have seizures exclusively at night may be eligible for a limited license, permitting daytime driving, even if a seizure occurred within the previous six months.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia only: Rule 375-3-5-.02 places anyone with an episode of altered consciousness 'in the preceding year' in Group B, which is ineligible for a regular license, but its table allows a limited license for Group B for 'Nocturnal epilepsy and stress hypoglycemia'. The rule does not say 'daytime driving'; the limitation is set by DDS on the medical review. No comparable South Carolina provision exists.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 375-3-5-.02 (Alterations of Consciousness), Group A/B table
verifiedClaims.note: Stamp as Georgia and soften 'permitting daytime driving' to 'a limited license' (the rule text does not specify daytime). Do not extend to South Carolina.

verifiedClaims.claim: Doctors may not be obligated to report patients with epilepsy, but they can report anyone with a known condition that impairs their ability to safely operate a vehicle.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: True in both states, and Georgia says so expressly. O.C.G.A. § 40-5-35: physicians 'may report to the department' any person with a disorder that would make them unable to drive safely; the report is confidential and 'No civil or criminal action may be brought against any person or agency for providing the information'. South Carolina has no statute requiring or addressing physician reporting of epilepsy (Title 56 Chapter 1 contains no epilepsy, seizure or lapse-of-consciousness provision); S.C. Code § 56-1-221(C) lets the driver, not the doctor, forward a physician's report to the Medical Advisory Board.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 40-5-35 (FindLaw text); S.C. Code Title 56 Chapter 1 (scstatehouse.gov, full text searched)
verifiedClaims.note: Replace 'may not be obligated' with the definite statement: 'Neither Georgia nor South Carolina requires a doctor to report a patient with epilepsy. Georgia expressly permits it and shields the reporting physician from liability (O.C.G.A. § 40-5-35).'

verifiedClaims.claim: Additionally, concerned individuals such as relatives, courts, judges, law enforcement officers, or citizens can submit non-anonymous letters to express their concerns. The DMV may then require the individual to undergo a medical evaluation and provide documented proof of their ability to drive safely.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: This is Georgia's process and the agency is DDS, not 'the DMV'. Georgia DDS Medical Review Process: requests 'may come from a non-anonymous relative, the court, law enforcement officer, judge, doctor, or concerned citizen'; DDS sends the Medical Form (DS-287) 'requesting a Medical Evaluation by a doctor', and a driver who does not comply within 30 days is notified that 'their driving privileges will be revoked in 30 days for medical reasons'. South Carolina's parallel is S.C. Code § 56-1-270: with 'good cause to believe that a person holding a South Carolina driver's license is incompetent or otherwise not qualified to be licensed because of physical or mental disability', the SCDMV 'may, upon written notice of at least ten days to the licensee, require him to submit to an examination', then 'may suspend or revoke the license ... or permit him to retain such license or may issue a license subject to restrictions'; refusal to submit is itself grounds for suspension or revocation.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Georgia DDS, Medical Review Process; S.C. Code § 56-1-270 (scstatehouse.gov); S.C. Code § 56-1-221(C)
verifiedClaims.note: Stamp the first sentence as Georgia (DDS), and add one sentence for South Carolina under § 56-1-270 / § 56-1-221. 'Provide documented proof of their ability to drive safely' is a fair lay rendering of the DS-287 medical evaluation.

verifiedClaims.claim: If a person has a seizure and causes an accident, it doesn't automatically make them legally responsible for the collision.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Eatmon v. Weeks, Nos. A13A0692/A13A0693 (Ga. App. July 16, 2013), quoting Lewis v. Smith, 238 Ga. App. 6 (1999); Collins v. Frasier, Op. No. 4385 (S.C. Ct. App. May 6, 2008), applying Boyleston v. Baxley, 243 S.C. 281 (1963)
verifiedClaims.note: Both states: an unforeseeable loss of consciousness is not negligence, and the driver bears the burden of proving it was unforeseeable (reused from facts-1707). SC opinion: https://www.sccourts.org/opinions/HTMLFiles/COA/4385.htm.

verifiedClaims.claim: Various factors come into play when determining liability, including the individual's history of epileptic events or seizures, whether they were under the care of a doctor for epilepsy, and whether they had been seizure-free for at least six months.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The legal test in both states is foreseeability: a driver who had prior warning of the condition cannot rely on the sudden-incapacity rule (Eatmon v. Weeks; Collins v. Frasier). Seizure history and medical care are exactly the evidence courts weigh. 'Seizure-free for at least six months' is not a liability element; it is Georgia's licensing standard (O.C.G.A. § 40-5-35), and driving inside that window, or against a doctor's advice, is evidence the seizure was foreseeable.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Eatmon v. Weeks (Ga. App. 2013); Collins v. Frasier (S.C. Ct. App. 2008); O.C.G.A. § 40-5-35
verifiedClaims.note: Keep the first two factors; reframe the third as 'whether they were driving inside Georgia's six-month no-seizure licensing window or against medical advice, which bears on whether the seizure was foreseeable'. Do not present the six-month figure as a South Carolina rule.

verifiedClaims.claim: While a seizure's involvement in the accident may attribute some fault to the person with the medical condition, the issue remains complex, particularly if they had no prior diagnosis or seizure history.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Eatmon v. Weeks (Ga. App. 2013) (no prior warning; summary judgment for the driver's estate); Collins v. Frasier (S.C. Ct. App. 2008) (no prior fainting history; verdict for driver affirmed)
verifiedClaims.note: Understated if anything: with no prior warning, Georgia courts have taken the case from the jury outright. Optional tweak only.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia uses a modified comparative negligence system to apportion fault between two or more parties whose negligence contributed to an accident. According to this system, if you were less than 50 percent at fault for the accident, you can still pursue compensation for the damages you sustained.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: profiles/writer-profile.md jurisdiction table; O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33(g)
verifiedClaims.note: Correct for Georgia. The section is Georgia-only on a two-state post; add South Carolina (see recommendedEdits).

verifiedClaims.claim: However, your level of recovery will be reduced by your fault percentage. For example, if you are found 10 percent liable for the accident, you can only receive 90 percent of the total value of your damages.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33(a) (damages reduced in proportion to the plaintiff's percentage of fault); same rule in South Carolina under Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243 (1991)
verifiedClaims.note: Arithmetic holds in both states.

verifiedClaims.claim: If it is determined that you are more than 50 percent at-fault for the accident, you cannot recover any damages.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia bars recovery at 50 percent or more, not 'more than 50 percent'. O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33(g): the plaintiff 'shall not be entitled to receive any damages if the plaintiff is 50 percent or more responsible for the injury or damages claimed'. A plaintiff found exactly 50% at fault recovers nothing in Georgia. South Carolina: recovery is barred only when the plaintiff's fault reaches 51% (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.), so a 50/50 plaintiff recovers half in South Carolina and nothing in Georgia.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33(g); profiles/writer-profile.md jurisdiction table (Georgia: less than 50%; South Carolina: less than 51%, Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.)
verifiedClaims.note: CONSEQUENTIAL. 'More than 50 percent' misstates Georgia's bar by exactly the case that matters (50/50) and contradicts the previous paragraph's 'less than 50 percent'. Change to '50 percent or more' and add the South Carolina rule. Never cite § 15-38-15 for the South Carolina bar.
